---
title: "On GitHub, not in files"
---

*Written for version 0.1.14. Source: [GitHub workflow](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow/blob/main/plugin/references/github-workflow.md), [collaborator onboarding](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow/blob/main/plugin/references/onboarding.md), [initialization questions](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow/blob/main/plugin/references/initialization.md), [initialize-analysis skill](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow/blob/main/plugin/skills/initialize-analysis/SKILL.md), [onboard-collaborator skill](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow/blob/main/plugin/skills/onboard-collaborator/SKILL.md), [shared conventions](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow/blob/main/plugin/references/conventions.md), [AGENTS.md template](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow/blob/main/plugin/assets/AGENTS.md).*

Some of a project lives in GitHub itself rather than in the repository's files: the settings that protect the main branch, the switch that puts the website online, and the issues, pull requests and milestones where work is discussed and tracked. This page explains each one, who can set it up, and what the assistant does with it. Several steps can only be done by a person with the right permission on the repository; the assistant can describe them but cannot do them.

| Step | Who can do it |
|---|---|
| Protect the main branch | The maintainer (admin rights on the repository) |
| Turn on GitHub Pages | Someone with admin or maintainer permission |
| Merge a pull request | A person; never an agent |
| Create tags and releases | The maintainer, or someone they explicitly authorise |
| Transfer the repository | Its owner; the new owner must accept |

## Protecting the main branch

**What it is.** A setting on GitHub that makes every change reach the main branch through a pull request. (The main branch is the one the project treats as current; GitHub calls it the *default branch*, and its name varies from project to project.) The plugin never renames it unless the maintainer asks.

**Why.** Each change is visible before it lands. That includes changes made by an AI agent working through a person's GitHub account, which GitHub treats as that person.

**Who does it.** The maintainer, once per repository. Setting up a project with the plugin includes this as a step for the maintainer. Agents do not change repository settings; they describe the steps for the person who can.

**What the plugin's steps say.** The maintainer creates a branch ruleset on GitHub (**Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New ruleset → New branch ruleset**) that:

- is named (for example "Protect default branch") and set to **Active**;
- targets the default branch;
- restricts deletions, blocks force pushes, and requires a pull request before merging;
- requires as many approvals as the team wants. A maintainer working alone uses 0, because GitHub never lets the author of a pull request approve it;
- leaves the bypass list empty unless the team decides otherwise. Anyone on that list can push straight to the branch, and so can any agent acting through their account.

A maintainer who works in R can do the same from the R console. The plugin gives a short check that reads the repository's settings and reports whether the branch is protected, and the matching command. The person runs these; agents only suggest them. The check can be rerun at any time, for example after the repository moves to a new owner.

**A limit.** On the free GitHub plan, a private repository cannot use rulesets. The plugin assumes a public repository and says so if someone plans a private one.

## GitHub Pages

**What it is.** The GitHub feature that puts the project website online. The website is built from the repository, but it goes live only after GitHub Pages is turned on.

**Who turns it on.** Someone with admin or maintainer permission on the repository. When a project is set up, the assistant reminds the person setting up that this step is needed, or the site will not appear. Agents cannot change the setting; they tell the person who can.

**When, for each publishing route.** During setup the project chooses how the site is published, and `AGENTS.md` records the choice.

| Publishing route | When to turn on Pages | What to choose |
|---|---|---|
| The rendered site (the `docs/` folder) is committed to the repository. This is the default. | Once the first pull request containing `docs/` has been merged | The default branch and the **/docs** folder |
| A GitHub Actions workflow builds and publishes the site, and `docs/` is not committed | Once the workflow has run on the default branch and created the `gh-pages` branch | The `gh-pages` branch and the **/ (root)** folder |

On the website, both routes start at **Settings**, then **Pages**, then **Source: Deploy from a branch**. A maintainer working in R can turn on Pages for the `docs/` route with one `usethis` command that the plugin gives. The workflow route needs a publish workflow file, which the plugin does not yet provide.

**A limit.** As with branch protection, a private repository on the free GitHub plan has no GitHub Pages.

## Issues

**What they are.** GitHub issues hold three kinds of open item:

- **Decision issues**: one open scientific question each, settled only by a named decider (see [The plan and its decisions](plan-and-decisions.qmd)).
- **Gaps between code and plan**: places where the code does not yet do what the plan says.
- **Known defects**: things that are wrong.

**Labels and templates.** Each project chooses its own labels, templates and conventions. The plugin prescribes none.

**What the assistant does with them.** It drafts a decision issue for each choice the plan leaves open, rather than choosing. Before asking anyone a question, it looks in the issues (and the plan, `AGENTS.md` and pull requests) for the answer. Before posting a comment as a person, it shows them the exact text and waits for their go-ahead, unless their own instructions say otherwise.

**For someone joining or taking over.** The open issues, with the plan and the open pull requests, are where a newcomer finds the project's state. The assistant starts there, not from the previous person's files or chats.

## Pull requests

**What they are.** A pull request offers a set of changes, made on a separate branch, for merging into the main branch. Any tool that creates a branch and opens a pull request will do; each person uses what they prefer, and the plugin does not prescribe one.

**The rules.** Good practice for everyone, and required of agents:

- **One branch per piece of work**, not one per commit.
- **Based on the main branch.** If a change needs another that has not been merged yet, wait for that one to merge, or fold both into one pull request. Pull requests are not stacked on each other, so no one is left to work out an order to merge them in.
- **The website follows the change.** When `docs/` is committed, the site is re-rendered on the same branch as the change it reflects.
- **It says what it addresses and what was checked.** Each pull request names the plan section or issue it addresses. It says what was checked, from the list in the project's `AGENTS.md` (for example: does the change follow the plan and leave every open decision open; does it avoid any number that could come from restricted data). A pull request opened by an agent also says whether the checks were done by running code on synthetic data or by reading only, and never calls synthetic results "results".
- **Closing a decision issue.** A pull request that settles a decision issue includes the plan change and the line `Closes #<n>`, where `<n>` is the issue's number. GitHub then closes the issue when the pull request is merged.

**Who merges.** A person. An agent may commit to a branch and open a pull request, but never merges one.

## Milestones (optional)

**What they are.** A milestone groups issues and pull requests under one phase of the project, with a target date, so anyone can see what that phase is waiting on. A decision issue placed in a milestone shows which phase it holds up. GitHub's Milestones page shows each milestone's due date and how many of its items are closed.

**Who chooses.** Milestones are optional. During setup the assistant asks whether the project wants them. If so, the team gives the phases and dates; for example, plan locked, cohort built, models fitted, manuscript drafted.

**What the assistant does.** If its GitHub connection can create milestones and assign items, it may do this once the person has given the phases and dates. Otherwise it walks them through the steps on the GitHub website.

## The setup note and check-ins

**The setup note.** Setting up a project asks one question at a time, and can stretch over several sessions. The assistant records the setup decisions made so far, and the questions still open, in one place the project agrees on: a setup note, or a tracker the project already uses. Nothing sensitive goes there, and no one's personal permissions. A later session resumes from this record instead of asking everything again.

**Saving unfinished work.** At the end of a working session, the assistant asks whether anything unfinished should be saved to the repository: a draft pull request, an issue comment marked as a draft, or a new issue. A new chat will not remember it. Anything holding results from restricted data that are not cleared for release stays where it is, and the person is told why.

**Check-ins (optional).** Anyone, whatever their role, can ask for a periodic check-in, using the assistant's scheduled tasks where the assistant has them. The person chooses how often it runs. It always reports what is waiting on them:

- issues assigned to them;
- decisions they make, each with the question, each option in a line, and a link to the decision issue. They can decide from the check-in or open the issue, but the decision itself is recorded in the issue;
- pull requests awaiting their review.

They can also choose to include what they are waiting on from others, work with no recent activity, and milestones due soon. The check-in can look over their recent chats for drafts that never reached the repository, and, if they have email connected and want it, their project email, proposing where to record each decision or request it finds. It reads the repository; it may draft messages but never sends or posts anything on its own. The person's check-in choices are kept in their own instructions, not in the project's shared files.

**Leaving a project.** When someone leaves or hands over work, the assistant goes through it with them before their last session: moving anything that exists only in a chat, on a laptop or in email into the repository (subject to the project's disclosure rules); deciding for each open issue and pull request whether to finish it, hand it on, close it with a reason, or mark it paused with what it is waiting on; and recording requests to others that have no answer yet. Not everything can be finished or given an owner, and a project may go dormant; the assistant records what stays open and why.

**Transferring ownership.** If the person leaving owns the repository, the assistant raises transferring it to the PI. The plugin's steps are **Settings → General → Transfer**, and the new owner must accept within a day. Issues, pull requests and history move with the repository, and old links to the repository redirect to the new one.

**The website caveat.** GitHub does not redirect the website. After a transfer, someone must update the site and repository links in `_quarto.yml`, the site pages and the README, re-render the site, and turn GitHub Pages on again under the new owner.
